figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) The storage graph G6 4 : a disjoint union of four hexagonal cycles (nc = 6), each storing one block of the target phase-difference pattern Φ as edge labels. Edges are colored by cycle: C1 (blue), C2 (red), C3 (green), C4 (purple). The cycles share no nodes or edges, so each carries an independent winding number ka. (b) The stored pattern Φ grouped by cycle, showing each cycle’s phase-difference vector. Each row corresponds to one cycle and is color-matched to the graph on the left. Five of each cycle’s six edge phases are free pattern variables; the sixth (closing) edge is fixed by the winding, so all six phases sum to 2π (winding ka = 1). The resulting configuration is an exponentially stable phase-locked configuration of the Kuramoto dynamics.

Figure 2: Anatomy of one routing cycle of (6). (a) At a vertex α = ek: the fast layer settles to ϕ(k) exactly; recognition saturates, q̃ → ek for γ large; the integrator r → ek on timescale τr; and the routing K⊤r peaks on the column K·,k. Under a permutation K this peak is unique at the next prescribed memory, and the replicator drives α toward the corresponding vertex. (b) During a transition: as α leaves ek, w(α) blends and θ∗(α) deviates from ϕ(k); δ(θ) is far from every signature, so the softmax q̃ is approximately uniform; r remains near ek, and V rises on the transient, closing the gate g. Both effects keep the replicator quiescent. (c) Plateau consolidation: as α approaches the next vertex the fast layer relocks and g reopens, but for a window of length ∼ τr the routing target K⊤r still favors the previous memory, so the replicator drives α toward the new vertex rather than prematurely advancing; once r catches up, the routing rotates forward and the next transition begins. (d) Closed-loop memory sequence: composition of vertex-to-next-vertex flows traces a memory sequence in (θ, r, α) whose combinatorial type is determined by K; for K a cyclic permutation this memory sequence is a heteroclinic cycle traversed indefinitely.

Figure 4: Mean dwell time as a function of τr (β = 15, τ = 80 fixed; N = 6, M = 5, cyclic routing). Solid line: closed-form upper bound (7). Markers: empirical mean over independent trials. The bound correctly predicts the linear scaling with τr but overestimates the empirical values by a roughly constant offset, attributable to two conservative assumptions in the derivation: (i) recognition lag and replicator activation are treated as strictly sequential, whereas they overlap in practice; and (ii) the formula uses the εtol-exit criterion, while the simulation detects transitions at the earlier argmaxj αj switch.

Left: selected pattern j∗(t) = argmaxj αj(t) as a step function; background shading identifies the active pattern by color. Center: attention weights αj(t). Right: soft routing matrices K(s) (Dirichlet-sampled, zero diagonal); dominant entries 0.59–0.95 encode each context’s successor graph with naturally varied non-successor entries. (A) K = K(0) (weekday): autonomous cycle 0→ 1→ 2→ 3→ 0 → · · · , mean dwell ≈ 460. (B) K = K(1) (weekend): same catalog, same oscillator weights, different cycle 0→2→3→1→0→· · · , mean dwell ≈ 555. (C) Mid-run switch K(0)→K(1) at t = 3200 (dashed line): blue region follows the weekday order; after the switch the system immediately redirects — from pattern 3 it goes to 1 (weekend: 3→ 1) instead of 0 (weekday: 3→ 0), then continues 1→ 0→ 2→· · · following K(1), with no change to any stored pattern or oscillator weight.
